ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's foreign ministry said Wednesday that it has lodged a "strong" protest with the U.S. ambassador over missile attacks conducted on Pakistani soil by unmanned drones. The aftermath of a suspected U.S. drone attack on a building in North Waziristan. The ministry said it summoned Ambassador Anne Patterson to underscore that such attacks violate Pakistan's sovereignty and should be stopped immediately. A statement from the ministry said Patterson was also told that the attacks have cost lives and undermined public support for Pakistan's counter terrorism efforts. The ministry lodged its protests three days after a missile strike from a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Pakistan has repeatedly raised objections to foreign nations violating its sovereignty to pursue terrorists. A U.S. ground operation in September that left several civilians dead rankled relations between the two countries. Last week, Pakistan's parliament passed a resolution that condemned any incursion on Pakistani soil by foreign forces. The resolution called for a review of the country's national security strategy and said the government needs to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ministry said it handed Patterson a copy of the resolution. The U.S. and NATO, which have troops in Afghanistan, have been seeking a way to effectively battle militants who launch attacks from Pakistan's swath of tribal areas along the border. They have become frustrated with Islamabad over the years, saying it is not being proactive enough against militants -- a claim Pakistan denies. The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from drones, which are controlled remotely. In another development, suspected Taliban militants kidnapped three government officials from an administrative office in Pakistan's tribal region Wednesday, officials said. The militants abducted two employees and a security guard from the Ambar district in Mohmand Agency. Mohmand is in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where U.S. and Pakistani officials have reported a presence of militants. Earlier in the day, militants tried unsuccessfully to take control of a school in Mohmand and abduct about 100 students, authorities said. A shootout with Frontier Corps followed, in which one militant was killed and another arrested. The Frontier Corps is a paramilitary force which uses recruits from Pakistan's tribal areas and is overseen by Pakistani army officers. Also Wednesday, a suicide car bomber detonated explosives outside a police checkpoint in northwest Pakistan, killing two security personnel, officials said. The Wednesday afternoon attack in the Bannu district of the North West Frontier Province also wounded a dozen people, military sources said. The bomber targeted a check point near a military hospital, said the sources who did not want their names revealed because they are not authorized to speak to the media. CNN's Reza Sayah and journalist Janullah Hashimzada contributed to this report .

Pakistan's foreign ministry has lodged a strong protest with U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson, condemning the ongoing missile attacks conducted by unmanned drones within Pakistani territory. In a pointed communication with the ambassador, ministry officials characterized these strikes as flagrant violations of Pakistan's sovereignty and demanded that such operations be halted immediately. The protest reflects mounting frustration within Pakistan's government over what it views as unilateral military action being carried out on its soil without proper authorization or consultation.

In its statement, the foreign ministry underscored the human cost of these drone operations, emphasizing that the strikes have resulted in significant loss of life among Pakistani civilians and combatants alike. Beyond the immediate casualties, officials warned that the attacks are actively undermining domestic support for Pakistan's own counter-terrorism initiatives. The ministry suggested that each strike erodes public confidence in the government's ability to protect its citizens and complicates efforts to build a national consensus against militancy, as many Pakistanis increasingly view the drone campaign as an affront to national sovereignty rather than a legitimate security measure.

This formal protest was issued just three days after a particularly deadly missile strike, believed to have been carried out by a U.S. drone, targeted a compound in South Waziristan. That attack resulted in the deaths of 20 people, further intensifying public and political pressure on Islamabad to take a firmer stance against the continuation of such operations.

The timing of this protest is also significant, coming on the heels of a resolution passed by Pakistan's parliament the previous week. That resolution explicitly condemned any incursion onto Pakistani soil by foreign military forces and called for a comprehensive review of the country's national security strategy. Underscoring the seriousness of this legislative action, a copy of the resolution was formally presented to Ambassador Patterson during the protest, signaling that the government's objections are backed by broad political consensus rather than being an isolated diplomatic gesture.

These developments illustrate the deepening strain in U.S.-Pakistan relations, as both countries grapple with fundamentally different approaches to counter-terrorism in the region. The United States and its NATO allies continue to search for effective strategies to combat militant networks operating from Pakistan's tribal areas along the Afghan border, and have repeatedly accused Islamabad of failing to take sufficiently proactive measures against these groups. This disagreement over strategy and sovereignty has created a persistent point of friction, with Washington viewing drone strikes as a necessary tool against an urgent security threat, while Pakistan increasingly frames them as a violation of its territorial integrity that undermines rather than strengthens the broader fight against extremism.

# Pakistan Summons U.S. Ambassador Over Drone Strikes, Lodges Formal Protest

**ISLAMABAD** — Pakistan's Foreign Ministry summoned the United States ambassador on Thursday to lodge a formal protest over a series of drone strikes in the country's tribal regions, the latest flashpoint in the often-strained relationship between the two nations over American counterterrorism operations conducted on Pakistani soil.

Ambassador officials were called to the ministry following strikes in North Waziristan that Pakistani officials say killed a number of people, including civilians, in the semi-autonomous tribal region bordering Afghanistan. Islamabad has long objected to the strikes, arguing they violate the country's sovereignty and undermine efforts to combat militancy through cooperation rather than unilateral military action.

"These attacks are a violation of Pakistan's territorial integrity," a Foreign Ministry statement said, echoing language used in previous protests. "Such actions are counterproductive and only serve to inflame public sentiment against the ongoing fight against terrorism."

The strikes are part of a broader U.S. campaign using unmanned aircraft to target militant commanders believed to be planning attacks against American and coalition forces in neighboring Afghanistan, as well as networks accused of plotting international terrorist operations. Washington has consistently maintained that the program is a critical tool in degrading militant networks operating in the rugged tribal belt, an area where Pakistani government authority has historically been limited.

Local officials in the tribal areas said the recent strikes targeted compounds believed to be used by militants linked to the Haqqani network and other insurgent groups. Casualty figures remain difficult to verify independently, as journalists and international observers have limited access to the remote region. Pakistani intelligence officials cited by local media put the death toll from the latest round of strikes in the double digits, with conflicting reports on how many of those killed were militants versus civilians.

Human rights organizations have repeatedly called for greater transparency regarding drone operations, criticizing both the U.S. and Pakistani governments for a lack of clear accounting of civilian casualties. Rights groups have documented cases in which strikes hit family compounds and gatherings, sparking outrage among local tribal communities and fueling anti-American sentiment.

Publicly, Pakistani officials have condemned the strikes, with parliament having previously passed resolutions demanding an end to the drone campaign. Privately, however, U.S. officials have long asserted — and some Pakistani officials have historically acknowledged in unofficial capacities — that elements of the two governments have cooperated on aspects of the targeting program, particularly in its earlier years, complicating the public narrative of unilateral American action.

The U.S. Embassy in Islamabad did not immediately issue a detailed response to the protest, though American officials have historically defended the program as compliant with international law and essential to national security interests, emphasizing precautions taken to minimize civilian harm.

The renewed diplomatic friction comes at a sensitive time, with the two countries navigating a complicated relationship shaped by shared counterterrorism interests, disagreements over Afghan policy, and Pakistan's broader economic reliance on Western financial institutions and allies.

Analysts say the protest is unlikely to result in a significant policy shift from Washington but reflects the ongoing political pressure Pakistani leaders face domestically to be seen pushing back against strikes that remain deeply unpopular among the public.

The Foreign Ministry said it would continue to raise the issue "at the highest levels" and called for the U.S. to respect Pakistani sovereignty in any future counterterrorism operations conducted near or within its borders.

*This is a developing story.*

# Pakistan Summons U.S. Ambassador Over Drone Strike Sovereignty Concerns

**Islamabad** — Pakistan's Foreign Ministry summoned the United States Ambassador on [date] to lodge a formal protest against recent drone strikes conducted in the country's tribal regions, which officials described as a violation of Pakistani sovereignty and international law.

## Diplomatic Protest

According to a statement issued by the Foreign Ministry, the ambassador was informed that the strikes—carried out in areas along the Afghan border—were "unacceptable" and undermined the bilateral relationship between Islamabad and Washington. The ministry reiterated calls for the U.S. to immediately halt unilateral drone operations within Pakistani territory, emphasizing that such actions bypass established channels of cooperation on counterterrorism.

"These strikes are a clear violation of Pakistan's territorial integrity," a senior Foreign Ministry official said. "We have consistently urged our American partners to respect our sovereignty while we continue to combat militancy through our own security operations."

## Parliamentary Resolution

The diplomatic move follows a resolution passed by Pakistan's Parliament, which condemned the continued use of drone strikes on Pakistani soil and called for an end to what lawmakers termed "extrajudicial killings" that have resulted in civilian casualties. The resolution, passed with rare cross-party support, demanded that the government take concrete steps—including a review of NATO supply routes—if the strikes continue.

Opposition and treasury benches alike voiced concerns that the strikes fuel anti-American sentiment and complicate Pakistan's own counterinsurgency efforts in the tribal belt, where the military has been engaged in operations against militant strongholds.

## Backdrop of Militant Violence

The protest comes amid a spate of militant attacks in Pakistan's tribal areas, which have strained security forces already stretched thin by operations against groups including the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and affiliated networks. Recent assaults on security checkpoints and convoys have killed and injured several soldiers and civilians, prompting renewed debate over the effectiveness of the current counterterrorism strategy.

Analysts note the complex dynamic at play: while Pakistan publicly condemns U.S. drone strikes, some officials privately acknowledge shared intelligence in targeting high-value militant commanders. This has fueled criticism from human rights groups and local communities in the tribal areas, who report civilian casualties and displacement as a result of both militant violence and airstrikes.

## U.S. Response

The U.S. Embassy in Islamabad has not issued a detailed public response to the summons, though American officials have previously defended drone operations as a necessary tool in targeting militant leadership that poses direct threats to regional and international security.

Washington has maintained that it consults with Pakistani counterparts on security matters, though it has stopped short of confirming or denying specific strike operations, citing the classified nature of such missions.

## Looking Ahead

The summons underscores persistent tensions in the U.S.-Pakistan relationship, particularly regarding counterterrorism cooperation and sovereignty issues. With Parliament pushing for stronger governmental action and continued instability in the tribal areas, observers suggest the coming weeks could see further diplomatic friction unless both sides find common ground on addressing militant threats without compromising Pakistan's territorial claims.

*This is a developing story. Further updates will follow as officials from both governments respond.*

**ISLAMABAD** — Pakistan's Foreign Ministry lodged a formal protest with the United States this week following a series of drone strikes in the tribal regions of North and South Waziristan, reigniting long-simmering tensions over the covert aerial campaign that has become a persistent irritant in bilateral relations.

## Foreign Ministry Response

In a statement released by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Pakistani officials characterized the strikes as a violation of the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity, reiterating a position the government has maintained through successive rounds of similar incidents.

"These attacks are a violation of Pakistan's sovereignty and territorial integrity," the ministry said, adding that such unilateral actions undermine the spirit of cooperation between the two countries and risk further alienating local populations in the tribal areas.

The statement called on the United States to cease drone operations within Pakistani territory, emphasizing that counterterrorism efforts should be conducted "with full respect for international law and in coordination with Pakistani authorities." Officials also warned that continued strikes could complicate efforts to stabilize the border regions and undermine public support for the broader counterterrorism partnership.

The U.S. Embassy in Islamabad, following standard practice, declined to confirm details of specific strikes, though Washington has historically maintained that such operations target high-value militant leaders operating in areas largely outside the control of Pakistani security forces.

## Background: A Fraught Partnership

The drone program in Pakistan's Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), particularly North and South Waziristan, has operated for years as one of the most contentious elements of the U.S.-Pakistan counterterrorism relationship. Washington has long viewed the strikes as a necessary tool against al-Qaeda, the Haqqani network, and Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants who use the rugged, mountainous terrain as a base for cross-border operations into Afghanistan.

Pakistani officials, however, have repeatedly characterized the strikes publicly as violations of sovereignty even as reports have periodically suggested tacit cooperation between the two governments behind closed doors. This dynamic — public condemnation paired with alleged private coordination — has fueled criticism from Pakistani political parties, religious groups, and human rights organizations who argue the strikes cause civilian casualties and fuel anti-American sentiment.

The tribal regions have served as a flashpoint since the mid-2000s, when the U.S. expanded its use of unmanned aerial vehicles as a central pillar of its counterterrorism strategy following the difficulty of conducting ground operations in the semi-autonomous areas. Pakistan's military has conducted its own operations in Waziristan, including large-scale offensives aimed at clearing militant strongholds, but has struggled to fully assert control over the region.

## Strains on the Bilateral Relationship

The latest protest comes amid a broader pattern of strain between Islamabad and Washington, with disagreements over drone policy compounding other friction points, including differences over Afghanistan policy, counterterrorism funding, and intelligence-sharing arrangements.

Analysts note that the Pakistani government faces a difficult balancing act: managing public outrage over strikes seen as violations of sovereignty while relying on U.S. military and economic assistance, and while militants operating from the tribal areas pose direct threats to the Pakistani state itself.

"Pakistan finds itself caught between domestic political pressure to resist perceived American overreach and the practical reality that militant networks in the tribal areas threaten Pakistani security as much as regional stability," said one regional security analyst who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters.

The Foreign Ministry's statement did not specify whether Pakistan would take further action beyond the diplomatic protest, though past incidents have occasionally led to temporary restrictions on NATO supply routes through Pakistani territory — a leverage point Islamabad has used previously to signal displeasure without severing cooperation entirely.

Neither government has indicated plans for de-escalation talks in the immediate aftermath of the latest strikes, leaving the drone issue as an unresolved fault line in one of the more complex bilateral relationships in the region.

*This report reflects statements from Pakistani officials and background context on the historical U.S.-Pakistan counterterrorism relationship.*
